summary: Specifies three sets of new ciphersuites for TLS that authenticate using pre-shared keys. The first uses only symmetric operations, the second adds a Diffie-Hellman exchange authenticated with the key, and the third combines public key authentication of the server with pre-shared key authentication of the client. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: If two people already share a secret handshake, they can use it to trust each other instead of showing ID. This memo lets secure web connections use such shared secrets.

subtitle: How TLS can authenticate with a secret both sides already hold, instead of certificates.

tldr.problem: TLS usually authenticates with public key certificates or Kerberos, which can be costly on small devices and awkward to manage in small closed setups.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines twelve new ciphersuites in three families (PSK, DHE_PSK and RSA_PSK) in which a symmetric key shared in advance is mixed into the premaster secret and the client names the key with a PSK identity.
tldr.outcome: Parties that already share a key can set up TLS without certificates or, depending on the family, without public key operations. The RFC warns that weak keys invite dictionary attacks and that only DHE_PSK gives Perfect Forward Secrecy.

today: RFC 4279 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 10015. Check those documents for changes that apply to the ciphersuites described here.

sections.title: Why Use Pre-Shared Keys
sections.content:
TLS normally authenticates with public key certificates or Kerberos. RFC 4279 describes how to use pre-shared keys (PSKs) instead: symmetric keys that the communicating parties shared in advance.

The RFC gives two reasons. First, depending on the ciphersuite, a PSK can avoid public key operations, which helps where CPU power is limited. Second, a PSK can be easier to manage in closed environments where connections are mostly configured by hand, or where the parties already have a way to set up a shared secret that can bootstrap a key for TLS.

The RFC defines three sets of ciphersuites. The PSK set uses only symmetric operations. The DHE_PSK set uses a PSK to authenticate a Diffie-Hellman exchange. The RSA_PSK set combines RSA and certificate authentication of the server with a PSK. All of them reuse existing cipher and MAC algorithms from RFC 2246 and RFC 3268.

The applicability statement says these ciphersuites are meant for a rather limited set of applications, usually with very few clients and servers. Alternatives it names are self-signed certificates with public key fingerprints, and the SRP ciphersuites, which protect against dictionary attacks but cost more computation.
sections.eli5: Usually a website proves who it is with a special ID card. Here, two sides already know the same secret word, so they can use that to trust each other without any ID card.

sections.title: The Plain PSK Key Exchange
sections.content:
The client signals that it is willing to use a PSK by listing one or more PSK ciphersuites in its ClientHello. If the server agrees, it picks one in its ServerHello. The Certificate and CertificateRequest messages are left out of the handshake.

Since either side may hold keys for several different parties, the client names the key it wants by sending a PSK identity in the ClientKeyExchange message. The server may help by sending a PSK identity hint in the ServerKeyExchange message; if there is no hint, that message is omitted. Both fields are opaque values of up to 2^16-1 octets.

The premaster secret is built from the PSK. If the PSK is N octets long, you concatenate a 16-bit value N, N zero octets, a second 16-bit value N, and the PSK itself. The handshake is then authenticated by the usual Finished messages.

If the server does not recognize the PSK identity, it MAY answer with an unknown_psk_identity alert. A server that wants to hide that fact MAY instead carry on as if the identity existed but the key was wrong, and answer with a decrypt_error alert.
sections.eli5: The visitor says which secret word they mean, like saying "it is the word we use for the clubhouse". Both sides then mix that word into their lock, and the lock only opens if they really both know it.

sections.title: DHE_PSK: Authenticating a Diffie-Hellman Exchange
sections.content:
The DHE_PSK ciphersuites run a Diffie-Hellman exchange and use the PSK to authenticate it. The RFC says this gives some additional protection against dictionary attacks and also provides Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS).

The ServerKeyExchange message now carries the identity hint plus the server's Diffie-Hellman parameters, and it is always sent, even when there is no hint. The ClientKeyExchange message carries the PSK identity plus the client's Diffie-Hellman public value.

The premaster secret is formed by doing the Diffie-Hellman computation as in other Diffie-Hellman ciphersuites of TLS, which yields a value Z. You then concatenate a 16-bit length of Z, Z itself, a 16-bit length of the PSK, and the PSK.
sections.eli5: Here the two sides first make up a fresh shared secret together, then use the old secret word to check that they were talking to the right person. Even if the old word leaks later, the fresh secret from today stays safe.

sections.title: RSA_PSK: Server Certificate Plus PSK
sections.content:
The RSA_PSK ciphersuites authenticate the server with RSA and certificates, in addition to using a PSK. As in normal RSA ciphersuites, the server must send a Certificate message. The identity hint in ServerKeyExchange is optional, and that message is omitted if there is no hint.

The client sends its PSK identity followed by an EncryptedPreMasterSecret: a 2-byte version number and a 46-byte random value, encrypted with the server's RSA public key. Both sides form the premaster secret by concatenating a 16-bit value 48, the version number and random value, a 16-bit length of the PSK, and the PSK. That makes it 52 octets longer than the PSK.

The RFC does not say what the certificates contain beyond the RSA public key, or how they are validated. It notes that RSA_PSK can be used with unvalidated self-signed certificates to get somewhat similar protection against dictionary attacks as DHE_PSK offers.
sections.eli5: The server shows an ID card and both sides know the secret word. The visitor locks a random number in a box only the server can open, so you need both the key to the box and the secret word to get in.

sections.title: Identities, Hints and Conformance
sections.content:
The RFC does not mandate any particular type of identity, but it does say how identities are encoded and what implementations must handle. A PSK identity MUST first be converted to a character string and then encoded to octets as UTF-8. For example, an IPv4 address is sent as dotted-decimal text such as 192.0.2.1, and a domain name in its usual text form, not in DNS protocol format. The RFC admits this encoding is not optimal but says it avoids identity-type-specific code. Servers are RECOMMENDED to run the identity through an appropriate stringprep profile before looking up the key.

On the identity hint, unless an application profile says otherwise, servers SHOULD NOT provide one and clients MUST ignore it.

TLS implementations MUST support arbitrary PSK identities up to 128 octets and arbitrary PSKs up to 64 octets, and longer ones are RECOMMENDED. A management interface must, unless a profile says otherwise, accept identities of up to 128 printable Unicode characters and PSKs of up to 64 octets entered as ASCII strings or in hexadecimal.
sections.eli5: The rules say how to write the name of the secret word so every machine reads it the same way, and that every machine must handle names and words at least a certain length.

sections.title: Ciphersuite Numbers and the New Alert
sections.content:
At the time, IANA had no registry for TLS ciphersuite or alert numbers, so the RFC asks IANA for nothing. It lists the twelve ciphersuite numbers for reference, from 0x00, 0x8A for TLS_PSK_WITH_RC4_128_SHA up to 0x00, 0x95 for TLS_RSA_PSK_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA. Each family is offered with RC4_128, 3DES_EDE_CBC, AES_128_CBC and AES_256_CBC, always with SHA.

The RFC also defines one new alert, unknown_psk_identity(115).
sections.eli5: Every combination gets a number, like a locker number, so both sides can say which one they mean. There is also a new warning message for "I do not know that secret word's name".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As with all shared-key schemes, the shared values need special care and limited exposure over time.

Forward secrecy. The PSK and RSA_PSK ciphersuites do not provide PFS. If the PSK (or, for RSA_PSK, both the PSK and the RSA private key) is compromised, an attacker can decrypt old conversations. DHE_PSK provides PFS if a fresh Diffie-Hellman private key is generated for each handshake.

Brute force and dictionary attacks. A short or human-chosen PSK may let an attacker recover it, offline from captured handshake messages or online by trying keys. With plain PSK, eavesdropping on a handshake is enough to get what an offline attack needs. With DHE_PSK the attacker must get a valid client to connect to them; passive eavesdropping alone is not enough. With RSA_PSK, only the server can get enough information. Implementations that let an administrator configure the PSK by hand are RECOMMENDED to offer generation of a new random PSK.

Identity privacy. The PSK identity is sent in cleartext, so an eavesdropper can identify the parties, and reusing the same identity over time may allow traffic analysis. The RFC notes this is no worse than client certificates, which are also sent in cleartext.
sections.eli5: If the secret word is too easy to guess, a sneaky person can just keep guessing. And the name of the word is shouted out loud, so listeners can tell who is talking to whom.
